newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Imperial Tobacco outlook as forecast.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Imperial Tobacco outlook as forecast.

text.p: Imperial Tobacco, in its first financial results since it was spun off from Hanson Plc last October, said on Wednesday its business outlook for the rest of the year was in line with its expectations.

The company, which owns the John Player Special and Embassy brands, reported profits before tax of 143 million pounds ($233 million) in the six months ended March 29, 1997 against brokers' forecast range of 136 to 150 million.

But looking to the longer term, chairman Derek Bonham said: "Against the background of a gradually declining U.K. market, the development of our international business remains fundamental to our future strategy."
Imperial's share of the British cigarette market grew to 38.4 percent from 37.9 percent, but the market showed signs of decline over the period.
The government budget last November pushed premium cigarette brand prices through three pounds per pack, turning many smokers to take up cheaper brands.
Imperial's Lambert & Butler brands in the low price sector continued to sell well, accounting for 12 percent of the British market.

Britain's cigarette market has fallen some three percent since the last budget with Imperial selling just under 15 billion sticks in that period. About 80 billion cigarettes are sold each year in Britain.

However, Imperial's profits from Britain rose five million to 147 million pounds in the six month period while profits from the groups overseas business grew 13 percent to 36 million, comprising 20 percent of total group profit.

"Our international volumes strengthened despite the strength of sterling and problems with our performance in France. To compensate for that we had increased sales in the southern European countries," said chief executive Gareth Davis in an interview.
"We see loads of opportunities for organic growth on the international side," said Davis.

Dutch cigarette paper producer Rizla International BV, which Imperial acquired in January, contributed 4.0 million pounds to group profits. Rizla has a presence in over 70 countries and a large market share in seven or eight European countries.
Analysts and investors say the future of the company depends on its ability to raise profits from overseas as cigarette sales continue to decline in Britain.

Imperial's French sales were hit by Rothman's launch of Winfield cigarettes, which sell for 22 francs for 30 against Imperial's John Player Special at 16.40 francs for 20, and a government moratorium on any changes to cigarette prices until after the election.
Total sales in France are down some four percent since the government increased duty on cigarettes in December 1996.

Davis said Imperial could benefit from improvements in production at Rizla and more efficient production at its main plant in Nottingham. In Nottingham eight ultra-high speed machines, capable of turning out 14,000 cigarettes every minute, will be installed by the end of the year and workers will move on to a three-shift pattern in a few days.
Davis called on the newly-elected Labour government to agree voluntary restrictions on advertising with the tobacco industry rather than imposing a ban by statute.
"If, as seems likely, there are going to be further restrictions on our marketing freedoms they should be voluntary rather than statutory.

Davis said it was unclear what the government's promise to ban all tobacco advertising in Britain meant. It seemed to include posters and press but possibly not cigarette makers' sponsorship of events.

He also argued against any further increase in tax on cigarettes. "Any further increase in excise taxes is only going to make for more down trading in the U.K. market and widen the gap in Britain's already punitive excise rate against the rest of Europe."
The company incurred a 40 million interest charge in the period from servicing 1.1 billion pounds of debt it inherited from Hanson as a result of its demerger.
Imperial shares were down half a penny at 401p in afternoon trade.
($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
